big: Rohan earns ₹12 lakh a year and has a ₹40 lakh home loan. His agent says ₹50 lakh of cover is plenty. Is it? Let us work it out instead of guessing.

lines: How do I know what cover I need? Everyone says a different number.
Start with a rule of thumb, then adjust for loans and savings. And remember that a fixed sum loses value over time.

note: A common rule of thumb is 10 to 15 times yearly income. Then adjust for loans, savings and your family's needs.

small: what ₹1 crore buys in 20 years at 6% inflation
h: A fixed sum loses buying power
alt: Bars showing the buying power of ₹1 crore shrinking over thirty years in lakh of rupees
caps: ₹1 crore of cover feels like a lot today.
At 6% a year, in 10 years it buys what ₹56 lakh buys today.
In 20 years, about ₹31 lakh in today's terms.
An assumed rate, not a forecast. Cover must be big enough to last.

q: Rohan earns ₹15 lakh a year. Using the 10 to 15 times rule, what is a sensible cover range to begin with?
opts: ₹5 crore, since more is always better
why: That is only one to two times his income, which would run out quickly for a family.
A flat number ignores his income, loans and family needs.
Far more cover than needed raises the premium without matching a real need.
Ten to fifteen times ₹15 lakh is ₹1.5 crore to ₹2.25 crore, a starting range to adjust.

q: Meena has a ₹30 lakh home loan. Why should her term cover consider it?
opts: It lowers her income, so smaller cover can do
So her family is not left holding the debt if she is gone
Banks always clear a home loan on the borrower's death
It makes the premium lower for the same cover amount
why: A loan does not lower her income. It is a liability that would remain.
Adding the loan to the cover lets the family clear it and keep the home.
A bank does not clear a loan on death unless a separate cover exists.
A loan does not lower the premium. It raises the cover she needs.

q: Rohan buys ₹50 lakh of cover for 30 years. Why might that become too little over time?
opts: Insurers reduce the sum assured every year
Term plans stop paying after ten years
Inflation shrinks what a fixed sum can buy
Premiums are added to the sum assured
why: The sum assured stays the same in rupees. It does not shrink by the insurer's choice.
A term plan pays for the whole term, not just ten years.
A fixed amount buys less as prices rise, so cover chosen today must allow for that.
Premiums are not added to the sum assured in a plain term plan.

q: Meena's savings and existing cover come to ₹20 lakh. How does this change the cover she needs?
opts: It lowers the extra cover needed, since part is already met
It adds to the need, since savings count as a liability
It has no effect, since cover is based on income alone
It doubles the cover needed, to protect those savings
why: Existing savings and cover already meet some of the family's need, so new cover can be lower.
Savings are an asset. They reduce the extra cover needed rather than raise it.
Income is a starting point, but savings and loans adjust the final figure.
Savings do not double the need. They reduce it, since they are already there.

pts: A rule of thumb is 10 to 15 times yearly income, then adjust.
Add loans, subtract savings and existing cover.
A fixed sum loses buying power, so do not under-buy.
